evidence.says: the brand began as Vick's Family Remedies, named for Dr. John Vick; sold as Wick in German-speaking countries because a German reader would say the V as /f/

evidence.source: Dictionary.com, Vick (the male given name, a form of Victor; same spelling as the surname)

notes: Today vˈɪks matches the surname Vick plus s, which is where the name comes from. Medium: no maker respelling; the reading rests on the name's origin, and nothing contradicts it. Not a dictionary word or given name (zipf 2.17). Nothing to ship.
review: evidence label only: Dictionary.com's 'Vick' entry is the given name (form of Victor), not the surname; reading, disposition and confidence unchanged

evidence.source: Dictionary.com (Random House), Visine: 'a brand of tetrahydrozoline'

alternatives.context: first-syllable main stress (VY-zeen), Dictionary.com's first-listed form

notes: Today's guess visˈini (vee-SEE-nee) adds a third syllable and reads the i as 'ee'; both sources give two syllables, 'vy' and 'zeen'. The sources split on which syllable carries the main stress (Dictionary.com lists VY-zeen first, then vy-ZEEN; Wikipedia vy-ZEEN), so both stresses are kept and the main one is the form two sources share; the other order is in alternatives. No maker respelling found (visine.com refuses automated fetches).

evidence.source: pronounce.tv (general pronunciation site; no source cited)

evidence.says: VOLTAREN  V OW1 L T ER0 AH0 N

notes: Today vˈOltəɹən (VOHL-tuh-ren). Low: no label, maker or dictionary respelling found (voltarengel.com and its help centre print none; Dictionary.com, Wiktionary and Merriam-Webster have no entry; Wikipedia gives only diclofenac; the 2020 OTC switch has no name review on Drugs@FDA). pronounce.tv agrees but cites nothing and contradicts itself elsewhere on the page; CMUdict agrees but is today's own source. The first vowel (vohl vs vahl) is the least certain part. The UK brand is Voltarol, so GB is British vowels on the US name. Nothing to ship.

evidence.source: Xyzal US site (Chattem/Sanofi), FAQs: 'How do I pronounce Xyzal®?'
evidence.says: two syllables (zi · zol) with an emphasis on the first syllable

alternatives.context: second vowel reduced (ZY-zul): today's reading; right if the maker's 'zol' is only a lay spelling of a weak vowel

notes: The maker confirms today's stress and 'zy'; it writes the second syllable 'zol', a full vowel the guide keeps (today zˈIzəl reduces it to 'zul'), kept with secondary stress as in Vraylar (d0014). Medium because the maker's lay respelling had to be interpreted: 'zi' is read 'zye' (the y of the spelling and today's reading) and 'zol' as 'zahl' (US lot vowel, GB ɒ). A reviewer may judge the second vowel a reduction difference and prefer already-correct. The Rx labels on DailyMed print no respelling.

evidence.source: Merriam-Webster Medical Dictionary, Zyrtec (trademark for cetirizine hydrochloride), seen in search-result text; the page refuses automated fetches

notes: Today's guess zˈɪɹtˌɛk says 'ZEER-tek'; Merriam-Webster's ˈzər is the 'fur' vowel (ZUR-tek), with secondary stress on 'tek' as today. Medium only because I could see the dictionary entry through a search result, not the page itself (as with Synthroid in d0014); a reviewer who can open the Merriam-Webster page could raise it to high. No label or maker respelling found (zyrtec.com refuses automated fetches; Dictionary.com, Wiktionary and Wordnik have no entry). The UK brand is Zirtek, so GB is British vowels on the US name.

evidence.source: ZzzQuil US site (Procter & Gamble/Vicks), home page and Safety & FAQs page
evidence.says: the maker writes it 'ZzzQuil' (no pronunciation given)
Zzz (the snoring sound, 'Z's') plus Quil from the same maker's NyQuil and DayQuil (NY-kwil, DAY-kwil)

notes: Low: no written pronunciation found (the maker's site and FAQ, Wikipedia, which redirects to diphenhydramine, and Wiktionary have none; my web-search allowance ran out before I could look for launch press coverage). Today zkwˈɪl has no vowel before 'kw' (a one-syllable 'zkwill'), so it is wrong whatever the intended reading. ZEE-kwil reads Zzz as one letter Z, stressed like its family names NyQuil and DayQuil; that is the usual spoken form as far as I know, but I have no source for it. A reviewer should check a ZzzQuil TV ad before shipping.
